name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Adopt **pre-approved model thresholds** set jointly by Engineering and Data Protection. This removes repeated debates over risk tolerance for each new model, cutting approval time from weeks to days. The trade-off is slower iteration for high-risk models, but the risk reduction justifies the delay.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s pre-approved thresholds trade *consistency* for *brittleness*—they’ll fail when edge cases fall outside the agreed scope, forcing emergency overrides that reintroduce the very debates they aimed to end. A better fix: keep the joint thresholds but add a *fast-track override* for high-risk models, with a post-deployment review within 48 hours; this keeps risk in check without locking the door on innovation. Settle the argument with a pilot: run the override for one quarter, measure how often it’s used and how often it prevents real harm.

name: Chisel
text:
Adopt Scriv’s fast-track override for high-risk models while keeping Reel’s pre-approved thresholds. This keeps the speed and consistency benefits for low-to-medium risk models while avoiding the brittleness trap Scriv warned about. The trade-off is a small increase in review complexity for high-risk cases, but it prevents emergency overrides from derailing the whole system. Engineering and Data Protection should co-own the override rules to balance speed and risk.
[dispatched 3 workers: worker-3008, worker-6786, worker-5118 — done, dissolved]

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s hybrid still hides the core failure: **Data Protection’s override power isn’t a speed bump—it’s a black-box escape hatch.** The fast-track doesn’t fix the root problem; it just relocates the debate to "emergency mode," where the same thresholds get ignored under pressure. The real fix: **require Data Protection sign-off for *any* override**, not just high-risk models, and publish the override reasons publicly. That settles it—no hidden overrides, no hidden risks.
